**Proposed mechanism:** CPS1 (HGNC:2511) —PRODUCES→ Carbamoyl Phosphate (CHEBI:17057); Carbamoyl Phosphate (CHEBI:17057) —LEADS_TO→ Urea Cycle (REACT:R-HSA-70307); Ammonia (CHEBI:16077) —LEADS_TO→ Urea Cycle (REACT:R-HSA-70307); Urea Cycle (REACT:R-HSA-70307) —DISRUPTS→ Hyperammonemia (HP:0002139); Urea Cycle (REACT:R-HSA-70307) —DISRUPTS→ Neurological dysfunction (HP:0001270); ASL (HGNC:829) —PRODUCES→ Argininosuccinate (CHEBI:17420); Argininosuccinate (CHEBI:17420) —LEADS_TO→ Urea Cycle (REACT:R-HSA-70307); Urea Cycle (REACT:R-HSA-70307) —DISRUPTS→ Hyperammonemia (HP:0002139); Urea Cycle (REACT:R-HSA-70307) —DISRUPTS→ Neurological dysfunction (HP:0001270). Mutations in CPS1 lead to a loss of function of the CPS1 enzyme, impairing the production of carbamoyl phosphate. Similarly, mutations in ASL lead to a loss of function of the ASL enzyme, impairing the synthesis of argininosuccinate. **Why it matters:** Understanding the shared urea cycle defect in argininosuccinic aciduria and carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I deficiency disease highlights the potential for therapeutic strategies targeting ammonia reduction or urea cycle support that could benefit patients with either condition.

Deficiency in ASL (argininosuccinic aciduria) impairs the cleavage of argininosuccinate, leading to its accumulation and reduced production of arginine and fumarate within the urea cycle. This leads to a depletion of ornithine within the mitochondria, hindering citrulline synthesis and thus slowing the entire urea cycle, also resulting in hyperammonemia and neurological impairment.

**Why it matters:** Understanding the shared pathway of ammonia detoxification, despite distinct genetic origins, is crucial for developing targeted therapies for hyperammonemic disorders. Strategies aimed at reducing ammonia levels or enhancing alternative detoxification pathways could benefit patients with either condition.
